segments.text: Euclid's Elements, Book One, Proposition Five. In an isosceles triangle, the angles at the base are equal, and if the equal sides are extended, the angles under the base are equal. Given isosceles triangle A B C with side A B equal to side A C, and sides A B and A C extended to D and E, we prove that angle A B C equals angle A C B, and angle C B D equals angle B C E.

segments.text: First, by Postulate Two, extend segment A B to B D, and extend segment A C to C E. Second, take a point F on B D, and by Proposition Three, cut off from the greater segment A E a segment A G equal to A F. Third, by Postulate One, construct segments F C and G B.

subsegments.text: First, by Postulate Two, extend segment A B to B D, and extend segment A C to C E. Second, take a point F on B D, and by Proposition Three, cut off from the greater segment A E a segment A G equal to A F. Third, by Postulate One, construct segments F C and G B.

segments.text: Now compare triangles A F C and A G B: since F A equals G A, A C equals A B, and they share the common vertex angle F A G, Proposition Four proves that base F C equals base G B, angle A C F equals angle A B G, and angle A F C equals angle A G B. Next, since the whole A F equals the whole A G, and within them A B equals A C, subtracting these equals by Common Notion Three leaves remainder B F equal to C G. Comparing the lower triangles B F C and C G B: since B F equals C G, F C equals G B, and angle B F C equals angle C G B, Proposition Four proves that the angles under the base, F B C and G C B, are equal, and angle B C F equals angle C B G. Finally, since the whole angle A B G equals A C F, and within them angle C B G equals B C F, subtracting these equals by Common Notion Three leaves angle A B C equal to angle A C B. Therefore in isosceles triangle A B C, the angles at the base are equal, and the angles under the base are equal, as was required to prove.
